title: Cumberland Falls
summary: Cumberland Falls, the “Niagara of the South,” drops about 68 feet over hard conglomerate on the Cumberland River and is known for its regular moonbow.
bodyMarkdown:
[Cumberland Falls](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cumberland_Falls) is called the "Niagara of the South." The Cumberland River drops about 68 feet here, in a curtain about 125 feet wide, on the line between Whitley and McCreary counties.

The falls are made by rock. The top layer is a hard sandstone and conglomerate, full of rounded pebbles, from the Pennsylvanian period, about 300 million years ago. Softer layers lie under it. Water wears away the soft rock faster, the hard cap breaks off in blocks, and the falls slowly move upstream. Geologists with the [Kentucky Geological Survey](https://kgs.uky.edu/kgsweb/olops/pub/kgs/GeoStory.pdf) think the falls began far downstream, near Burnside, and have backed up about 45 miles over a very long time. The gorge below is what they left behind.

The falls are famous for something else too. On clear nights near the full moon, the mist can catch the moonlight and make a [moonbow](https://grokipedia.com/page/Moonbow), a pale rainbow at night. Moonbows show up in other places, but Cumberland Falls is one of the few places in the world where they come with any regularity, and the park schedules moonbow nights around them.

People came to see the falls long before there was a park. In the 1800s a hotel stood nearby, and visitors made the rough trip by wagon and on horseback.

In the 1920s a power company wanted to dam the river for electricity. Many Kentuckians fought it. [T. Coleman du Pont](/people/#t-coleman-du-pont), a Kentucky-born businessman and former U.S. senator, offered to buy the falls and the land around them for a state park. He died in 1930 before the deal was done. His widow finished the purchase, and the family gave the land to Kentucky. The park was dedicated on August 21, 1931.

The Civilian Conservation Corps built trails and shelters in the 1930s, and DuPont Lodge, named for the family, opened later as the park's stone-and-timber lodge.

## Kentucky today

[Cumberland Falls State Resort Park](https://parks.ky.gov/corbin/parks/resort/cumberland-falls-state-resort-park), near Corbin, keeps the falls open to visitors year-round, with overlooks, trails, DuPont Lodge, and moonbow nights posted on the park calendar.
